title: Sachem Aquash of the Montaukett
summary: Aquash, also written Aquaas or Aquosh, was a late seventeenth-century Montaukett sachem whose recorded leadership appears in East Hampton and Montaukett land records during a period of colonial pressure on Montaukett land. Montaukett land-record sources first identify the sachem as Aquaas in 1684, and in 1687 Aquaas appears to have taken the name of his great-grandfather Wyandanch in a deed context. His life is only partly visible through surviving documents, but those records place him in Montaukett leadership.
content:
Aquash, also written Aquaas or Aquosh, was a late seventeenth-century Montaukett sachem whose leadership appears in East Hampton and Montaukett land records beginning in 1684. The sources cited here do not establish his exact birth or death dates.

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island, 2001, note discussing Aquaas/Aquosh in 1684 and the 1687 deed reference to Wyandanch.
  2. Donna Barron, The Long Island Indians and Their New England Ancestors.
why_this_matters: Aquash matters because even a brief record can show Montaukett leadership continuing after Wyandanch, Moshup, and other earlier sachems. His recorded name and the later use of Wyandanch show how colonial records preserved fragments of Native authority during land pressure and dispossession.
